title: Sharing memory-compression code: functional checks passed, performance unmeasured
headline: The shared compression library passed its required functional checks. A failure in the timing setup left its effect on speed unknown.

sections.title: Why make compression reusable?
sections.lead: Linux can save working memory (RAM) by compressing inactive application data. ZSwap is its existing compressed-memory cache; XSwap is this project's alternative swap design. XSwap currently relies on ZSwap for compression.

blocks.text: The goal is to let both systems use the same compression code. Later work would let XSwap operate independently and move stored data to disk when RAM is tight.

sections.title: 1. The system: keep application data available
sections.lead: A memory page is a fixed-size block of application data. When an inactive page is removed from active RAM, its contents must remain available in compressed RAM or on disk, ready to restore when needed.

blocks.takeaway: Compression saves RAM and spends processor time to restore data

blocks.text: This experiment changes the compression code inside RAM. Moving stored data from RAM to disk under memory pressure is a later stage.

sections.title: 2. The boundary: decisions versus compression
sections.lead: ZSwap decides which data to keep, tracks where it is stored and accounts for its memory use. The new library compresses, stores, restores and frees that data. XSwap still reaches the library through ZSwap at this stage.

blocks.takeaway: Separate storage decisions from the reusable compression work

blocks.text: ZSwap remains responsible for keeping stored data alive while another operation uses it. The library does the compression and storage work without taking over those decisions.

sections.title: 3. The change: extract one reusable library
sections.lead: Before the change, compression and storage code lived inside ZSwap. After the change, ZSwap calls a shared library named page_compress. The stored data format and the rules for tracking and freeing it stay the same.

blocks.takeaway: Move the compression implementation behind a reusable interface

blocks.text: Benefit: future callers can reuse one implementation. Cost: another interface to maintain and another allocation for each storage pool, the container for compressed data. The actual memory overhead and effect on speed remain unmeasured.

sections.title: Next: finish measurement and independent XSwap support
sections.lead: Keep the library as a development candidate. First make the timing setup reliable enough to compare the original and modified kernels. Separately, finish the test support needed for XSwap to use the library with ZSwap disabled.

blocks.takeaway: Each later step needs its own working implementation and evidence

blocks.text: Reject the next design if it corrupts data, miscounts memory or frees data still in use. Any speed claim requires repeatable measurements of both versions. Independent XSwap and pressure-driven disk migration have not run.

patches.takeaway: The caller keeps responsibility for tracking and freeing stored data
The library compresses a page and returns its storage reference
ZSwap delegates compression storage while preserving its existing lifetime rules
